blocks.text: 1. Why RAG Is Needed

blocks.alt: Frozen knowledge is fixed by RAG into fresh, external knowledge

blocks.text: What Is RAG closed by pointing toward this: the specific problems the architecture actually solves, which ground that earlier general definition in real, concrete motivation.
RAG grounds a model's answers in cases where plain generation alone falls short, for a handful of concrete reasons.
2. Recapping The Preview
Why RAG Is Needed was previewed in that earlier topic as the next stop for exploring the actual problems RAG solves.
This topic gives it the complete, dedicated treatment promised there, working through every detail only hinted at earlier.
3. Recapping The Two Stage Structure
RAG's retrieval and generation stages, covered in What Is RAG, exist for concrete, practical reasons.
The sections ahead spell out exactly what goes wrong without them.
4. The Frozen Knowledge Problem

blocks.alt: A training cutoff date means no knowledge of newer facts

blocks.text: A trained model's knowledge stops updating the moment training finishes.
Anything that happened or changed afterward is invisible to that frozen model, which is the first real problem RAG addresses.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Problem","What RAG solves"],"rows":[["Frozen knowledge","Retrieval surfaces information newer than training"],["Private data","Retrieval surfaces content never in training data at all"]]}

blocks.text: 5. The Private Data Problem

blocks.alt: Private company data is compared against public training data

blocks.text: Internal company documents or personal files were never part of any public training data.
A plain model has no way to know about that content at all, which is the second real problem RAG addresses.
6. Preview Of The Hallucination Problem
Without real, grounding information, a model sometimes fills gaps with confident, invented text.
Hallucinations, the next topic in this module, covers that specific failure in full.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: This sets up Hallucinations, the next topic in this module, as one specific, serious failure mode that RAG's grounding helps reduce.

blocks.text: 7. The Retraining Cost Problem

blocks.alt: Full retraining is compared against RAG, which just updates documents

blocks.text: Updating a model's frozen weights through retraining, covered in Retraining, costs real time and compute.
RAG sidesteps that cost entirely: updating the retrievable documents is far cheaper, which is the third real problem it solves.
8. Transparency And Citations

blocks.alt: A RAG answer comes with a source citation

blocks.text: A plain model's answer offers no way to trace where a claim actually came from.
RAG can cite the exact retrieved passage an answer relied on, which is the fourth real problem it solves.

blocks.text: 9. Cost Comparison RAG Versus Fine-Tuning

blocks.alt: Fine-tuning is expensive while RAG is cheaper to update

blocks.text: Fine-tuning, covered under LoRA and Full Fine-Tuning, bakes new knowledge directly into weights.
RAG keeps that knowledge external instead, trading some latency for far lower update cost, the fifth tradeoff worth understanding.
10. Recognizing Which Real Problems Point Toward RAG

blocks.alt: Having frozen or private knowledge points toward using RAG

blocks.text: RAG solves staleness and private data access together.
For stable, publicly known, general knowledge, the kind covered under Transfer Learning, a plain model alone remains sufficient.

blocks.text: 12. Common Mistakes

items: Assuming a plain language model automatically knows about recent events after its training cutoff.
Expecting a model to answer questions about private, internal documents it was never trained on.
Choosing full fine-tuning to add fast-changing information, when RAG updates far more cheaply.
Trusting an ungrounded answer without checking whether it can actually be traced to a real source.

blocks.text: 13. Key Takeaways

items: RAG solves specific, concrete problems that plain generation alone runs into.
A trained model's knowledge is frozen at training time; anything after that is invisible to it.
Private, internal documents were never part of public training data, so a plain model cannot know them.
Without grounding information, a model sometimes fills gaps with confident, invented text.
Updating a model's frozen weights through retraining costs real time and compute.
RAG sidesteps that cost by updating retrievable documents instead of the model itself.
RAG can cite the exact retrieved passage an answer relied on, unlike plain generation.
RAG trades some latency for far lower update cost compared to fine-tuning new knowledge into weights.
